dek: A gateway design for observable model traffic and a repair for AI evaluations with extended thinking.

stories.title: Langfuse explains how its gateway records coding-agent calls without translating provider APIs
stories.summary: Langfuse describes a Rust gateway that preserves native provider APIs, batches traces in the background and budgets memory for agent traffic.
body: Langfuse is an AI engineering platform for tracing and monitoring applications. Its gateway sits between coding agents and model providers, giving operators a way to record calls and see usage by key, user and team. The company says agent requests can be large, responses can remain open for minutes, and a gateway failure can interrupt the agents depending on it.

First, the gateway checks the key and model against the Langfuse control plane, caching the result. It forwards the provider's native API rather than translating between providers, then streams the response back. It batches traces for background ingestion so the response does not wait for them. Teams can choose usage-only records or full input and output capture; self-hosted administrators can turn recording off.

Langfuse chose Rust and its asynchronous runtime to spread work across cores and budget memory during bursts. Its own comparison used a mock provider and one repeated streaming request, with different gateway configurations; the company calls the results directional rather than a ranking. Native APIs also mean changing providers is not as simple as changing a model name, and there is no automatic cross-provider fallback. The gateway is in public beta and can be self-hosted.
stories.takeaway: Teams evaluating a model gateway can examine both trace capture settings and how provider-specific behavior is preserved.

stories.title: Phoenix fixes evaluator requests for Anthropic prompts with extended thinking
stories.summary: Server-side language model evaluators now adjust tool choice when an Anthropic prompt enables extended thinking, avoiding a rejected request.
body: Arize Phoenix is an open-source platform for observing and evaluating AI applications. Its server-side language model evaluators use a model to assess outputs. The maintainers found that an Anthropic evaluator request could fail when its prompt enabled extended thinking: the evaluator forced a tool call, a combination the API rejected with a request error.

The fix checks the invocation parameters before sending the evaluation request. When extended thinking is enabled, Phoenix now allows automatic tool choice and adds a system instruction naming the tool, instead of forcing the tool call. A thinking setting inside the extra request body takes precedence because that body is merged last. Adaptive or disabled thinking continues to use forced tool choice, which the maintainers say the API accepts.

The change applies to the evaluator path; the playground still sends the user's chosen tool setting. The linked change reports live API checks of affected and unaffected configurations, but does not quantify how often users encountered the failure.
stories.takeaway: Teams running Anthropic-based Phoenix evaluators can check whether extended-thinking configurations that previously failed now complete.
